materials.title: Listen to a talk in a music appreciation class.
materials.transcript: Have you ever wondered why music has such a strong emotional impact on us? Sometimes it comes from the way our brains respond to what's called dissonance. Dissonance occurs when two or more notes clash. They sound together in a way that creates tension or instability. Imagine hitting two piano keys that are right next to each other. It creates a sound that feels unresolved. Why does this matter? Well, music thrives on the tension between opposites. So dissonance is what creates a sense of unease that begs for resolution, to move to harmony. And when that resolution comes, say those two notes resolve into a harmonious chord, it feels like a breath of fresh air. This combination of tension and release forms the emotional push and pull of music. Here's something you might not know, though. The use of dissonance hasn't always been welcome. There were long periods in European history during which dissonance in music was considered sinful by the religious authorities at the time. But then in the 1700s, the German composer Johann Sebastian Bach came along. Bach started using dissonance more dynamically, and it became central to compositions. And today modern genres like jazz and experimental music rely heavily on the unique emotions dissonance creates. Let's listen to some modern pop music with some great examples.

materials.title: Listen to a talk in a film class.
materials.transcript: As you know, Hollywood, California, is associated with movies. Early Hollywood, through the 1920s or so, was the period of silent films, with no recorded dialogue. Maybe you've heard of Charlie Chaplin, a famous silent film star. He was prolific early in the century. Movies remained silent until the first full-length sound film with spoken dialogue throughout, The Jazz Singer. But The Jazz Singer came out later, not till 1926. One important filmmaker's career spanned the silent film era and later. Her name was Dorothy Arzner. Arzner's career was unusual for a woman at that time. I can think of maybe one other female director who had a long Hollywood career in those days. Dorothy Arzner started out by typing scripts and then editing film. Then, in 1922, she had an opportunity to edit and direct for a silent film called Blood and Sand. It irritates me that she was not credited as an editor or director for Blood and Sand. It's unfair. She made decisions that saved the movie studio thousands of dollars. She deserved acknowledgement. From there, Arzner made about 20 films and was credited for her work. In fact, she was the first woman to direct a sound film. Many of her films deal with, shall we say, unconventional romance stories: unexpected characters meeting, falling in love, getting married. Arzner's films introduced several women actors who would go on to become hugely successful in comedies and dramas themselves.

materials.title: Listen to a talk on an architecture podcast.
materials.transcript: The Great Pyramids of Egypt were basically built by piling one stone on top of another. Many of the stones used to build them contain huge numbers of one specific type of fossil shell. These shells resemble the size and shape of small coins, and the scientific name of the shells reflects this. The organisms that form these shells are called nummulites. That's a word with the same root as the word numismatics, which is the study of money. And coins are money, right? Okay, so considering that these shells, while small, are still large enough to collect in your hand, it may come as a surprise that they were created by a unicellular organism, a creature that consisted of just one single huge cell, not a multicellular organism like clams or oysters. Amazing, right? The vast numbers of these shell-making organisms once lived on a tropical seafloor millions of years ago in what's now Egypt. Over time, huge numbers of these shells were buried beneath many additional layers. The weight of the overlying layers compacted the limey sediment closer together until it turned into a solid rock known as limestone. But limestone that was rich in nummulites wasn't suitable for construction in all sections of the pyramids, so other types of stone had to be quarried as well. Okay, next up, let's look at the pyramid structure and why different kinds of stone were used for different parts.

materials.title: Listen to a talk on a history podcast.
materials.transcript: Have you had a zipper betray you—stuck halfway, misaligned, and suddenly you're negotiating with your jacket like it's got a personality? That kind of failure is annoying, but it's only noticeable because properly functioning zippers are seen as a given. The modest zipper is actually a big deal. When its earliest form was invented in the late 19th century, people weren't super impressed. Hooks and buttons had been around forever, and people thought they worked well enough. And the first versions of the zipper weren't sleek. They were fussy. They jammed. Basically, they malfunctioned much more commonly than they do today. In other words, they weren't a must-have. What made the zipper take off was a new design that was invented by a Swedish-American engineer named Gideon Sundback. Sundback's idea was to create uniform metal teeth. With these teeth, all of the exact same size, the slider could now reliably glide into place in a single motion. The zipper's impact on everyday life has been huge since designers of bags and clothing stopped planning around slow or fragile closures. Suitcases could now pack more stuff without being as bulky because luggage no longer needed unwieldy straps and buckles, so traveling became more convenient. Outdoor clothing became easier to seal with one hand. That meant you could close a pocket while holding something else. We're now so used to this convenience that we take it for granted.
